title: Book Nine (1812) — Chapter 3
paragraphs: Meanwhile the Emperor of Russia had spent more than a month in Vilna, reviewing troops and holding maneuvers. Nothing was ready for the war that everyone expected, the war the Emperor had come from Petersburg to prepare. There was no general plan of action. The wavering between the various proposed plans had even grown worse after the Emperor had been a month at headquarters. Each of the three armies had its own commander in chief, but no supreme commander led all the forces, and the Emperor did not take that role himself.

The longer the Emperor stayed in Vilna, the less anyone — tired of waiting — got ready for the war. All the efforts of the people around the sovereign seemed aimed at one thing: making him pass his time pleasantly and forget that war was coming.

In June, after many balls and fetes given by the Polish magnates, the courtiers, and the Emperor himself, one of the Polish aides-de-camp in attendance thought the Emperor's aides-de-camp should give him a dinner and ball. The idea was welcomed eagerly, and the Emperor agreed. The aides-de-camp raised the money by subscription. They invited the lady thought most pleasing to the Emperor to be hostess. Count Bennigsen, who owned land in the Vilna province, offered his country house for the fete, and the thirteenth of June was set for a ball, dinner, regatta, and fireworks at Zakret, Count Bennigsen's country seat.

On the very day Napoleon ordered the crossing of the Niemen, and his vanguard drove off the Cossacks and crossed the Russian frontier, Alexander was spending the evening at the entertainment his aides-de-camp were giving at Bennigsen's country house.

It was a gay, brilliant fete. Connoisseurs of such things said that rarely had so many beautiful women been gathered in one place. Among the Russian ladies who had followed the sovereign from Petersburg to Vilna was Countess Bezukhova, whose ample, so-called Russian beauty eclipsed the refined Polish ladies. The Emperor noticed her and honored her with a dance.

Boris Drubetskoy was there too. He had left his wife in Moscow and was for the time being en garçon (as he put it), and though he was no aide-de-camp, he had put a large sum toward the expenses. Boris was now a rich man who had risen to high honors. He no longer looked for patrons but stood on equal terms with the highest of his own age. He was meeting Helene in Vilna after a long time apart and did not think of the past. But Helene was enjoying the favor of a very important personage, and Boris had only recently married, so they met as good friends of long standing.

Dancing was still going on at midnight. Helene had no suitable partner, so she offered herself to dance the mazurka with Boris. They were the third couple. Boris looked coolly at Helene's dazzling bare shoulders, which rose out of a dark gauze gown embroidered with gold, and talked to her about old acquaintances. All the while, without knowing it himself and without anyone noticing, he never stopped watching the Emperor, who was in the same room. The Emperor was not dancing. He stood in the doorway and stopped couple after couple with the gracious words that only he knew how to say.

Just as the mazurka began, Boris saw Adjutant General Balashev, one of those closest to the Emperor, approach him and, against court etiquette, stand beside him while he was talking to a Polish lady. The Emperor finished speaking to her and gave Balashev a questioning look. He evidently understood that Balashev would act this way only for important reasons, so he gave the lady a slight nod and turned to him. Balashev had barely begun to speak when a look of amazement crossed the Emperor's face. He took Balashev by the arm and walked across the room with him, unconsciously clearing a path seven yards wide as people stepped aside on both sides. Boris noticed Arakcheev's excited face as the sovereign left with Balashev. Arakcheev looked at the Emperor from under his brow and, sniffing through his red nose, stepped out of the crowd as though expecting the Emperor to address him. (Boris understood that Arakcheev envied Balashev and was displeased that evidently important news had reached the Emperor some way other than through himself.)
But the Emperor and Balashev passed out into the lighted garden without noticing Arakcheev, who followed some twenty paces behind, holding his sword and glancing angrily about.

Throughout the figures of the mazurka, Boris was worried by one question: what news had Balashev brought, and how could he learn it before the others? In the figure where he had to choose two ladies, he whispered to Helene that he meant to choose Countess Potocka, who, he thought, had gone out onto the veranda. Then he glided across the parquet to the door that opened onto the garden. There he saw Balashev and the Emperor coming back toward the veranda, and he stopped. They were heading for the door. Boris, fluttering as if he hadn't had time to get out of the way, pressed himself respectfully against the doorpost with his head bowed.
The Emperor, agitated like a man who has been personally insulted, was finishing with these words:

"To enter Russia without declaring war! I will not make peace as long as a single armed enemy remains in my country!" It seemed to Boris that the Emperor took pleasure in saying this. He was pleased with how he had put his thoughts, but displeased that Boris had overheard.
"Let no one know of it!" the Emperor added with a frown.
Boris understood that this was meant for him, and closing his eyes, he bowed his head slightly. The Emperor went back into the ballroom and stayed about another half hour.

So Boris was the first to hear that the French army had crossed the Niemen. This let him show certain important personages that he often knew things hidden from others, and in that way he rose in their esteem.

The unexpected news that the French had crossed the Niemen was especially startling after a month of expectations that came to nothing, and at a ball. When the news first reached him, the Emperor, in his indignation and resentment, had hit on a phrase that pleased him, expressed his feelings fully, and has since become famous. He got home at two o'clock that night and sent for his secretary, Shishkov. He told him to write an order to the troops and a rescript to Field Marshal Prince Saltykov, and insisted that the words be put in that he would not make peace as long as a single armed Frenchman remained on Russian soil.
The next day this letter went to Napoleon:
Monsieur mon frère,

Yesterday I learned that your troops have crossed the Russian frontier, in spite of the loyalty with which I have kept my engagements to Your Majesty. This very moment I have received from Petersburg a note in which Count Lauriston gives me the reason for this aggression: Your Majesty has considered yourself at war with me ever since Prince Kurakin asked for his passports. The reasons the Duc de Bassano gave for refusing them to him would never have led me to suppose that this could serve as a pretext for aggression. In fact the ambassador, as he himself has declared, was never authorized to make that demand, and as soon as I was informed of it I told him how much I disapproved and ordered him to remain at his post. If Your Majesty does not intend to shed the blood of our peoples over such a misunderstanding, and agrees to withdraw your troops from Russian territory, I will treat what has passed as though it had not occurred, and an understanding between us will be possible. Otherwise, Your Majesty, I shall find myself forced to repel an attack that nothing on my part has provoked. It still depends on Your Majesty to spare humanity the calamity of another war.
I am, etc.,
(signed) Alexander
